claim: Genome-wide association studies have found variation within the complement factor H gene family links to host susceptibility to meningococcal disease caused by infection with Neisseria meningitidis.
source: Genome-wide association studies have found variation within the complement factor H gene family links to host susceptibility to meningococcal disease caused by infection with Neisseria meningitidis (Davila et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davila et al., 2010

claim: N. meningitidis subverts immune responses by hijacking complement factor H (CFH) to the bacterial surface.
source: N. meningitidis subverts immune responses by hijacking a host-immune regulator, complement factor H (CFH), to the bacterial surface (Schneider et al., 2006; Madico et al., 2007; Schneider et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schneider et al., 2006, 2009 and Madico et al., 2007

claim: Complement factor-H related 3 (CFHR3) promotes immune activation by acting as an antagonist of CFH.
source: We demonstrate that complement factor-H related 3 (CFHR3) promotes immune activation by acting as an antagonist of CFH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including haemolysis assays and bacterial survival assays

claim: The bacterium cannot sufficiently distinguish between CFH and CFHR3 due to conserved sequences between them.
source: Conserved sequences between CFH and CFHR3 mean that the bacterium cannot sufficiently distinguish between these two serum proteins to allow it to hijack the regulator alone.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data and binding affinity measurements showing similar KD values for CFH and CFHR3 binding to fHbp

claim: The level of protection from complement attack achieved by circulating N. meningitidis depends on the relative levels of CFH and CFHR3 in serum.
source: The level of protection from complement attack achieved by circulating N. meningitidis therefore depends on the relative levels of CFH and CFHR3 in serum.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent effects of CFHR3 on bacterial survival and CFH binding

claim: Case fatality rates for bacteraemic meningococcal disease remain at around 10%.
source: case fatality rates for bacteraemic disease remain at around 10%, and a significant proportion of survivors are left with long-term sequelae (Vyse et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vyse et al., 2013

claim: Up to 40% of the population are healthy carriers of N. meningitidis.
source: For most individuals, however, this human-specific bacterium is primarily a non-pathogenic commensal of the nasopharynx, and up to 40% of the population are healthy carriers (Caugant and Maiden, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caugant and Maiden, 2009

claim: Complement activation is critical for protection against meningococcal disease.
source: It is known, however, that complement activation is critical for protection against disease, evident from the susceptibility of individuals with genetic deficiency of either the alternative complement pathway (AP) or terminal pathway activation, and among those receiving therapy that prevents terminal pathway activation (Schneider et al., 2007; McKeage, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schneider et al., 2007 and McKeage, 2011

claim: N. meningitidis recruits CFH to its surface by expressing factor H binding protein (fHbp).
source: N. meningitidis recruits the human negative complement regulator, complement factor H (CFH), to its surface by expressing factor H binding protein (fHbp) (Schneider et al., 2006, 2009; Madico et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schneider et al., 2006, 2009 and Madico et al., 2007

claim: fHbp can be divided into three variant groups (V1, V2, and V3) which have >85% sequence identity within groups but only 60–70% similarity between groups.
source: fHbp can be divided into three variant groups (V1, V2, and V3), which have >85% sequence identity within the groups but only 60–70% similarity between groups (Masignani et al., 2003; Brehony et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Masignani et al., 2003 and Brehony et al., 2009

claim: fHbps from all variant groups bind CFH with a KD in the low nanomolar range.
source: fHbps from all variant groups bind CFH with a KD in the low nanomolar range (Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2012

claim: The only SNPs associated with meningococcal disease in a recent GWAS were those among the CFH–CFHR locus, including SNPs within CFH and CFHR3.
source: Therefore, it is significant that the only single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with meningococcal disease in a recent genome-wide association study (GWAS) were those among the CFH–CFHR locus. These included SNPs within CFH and the downstream gene, CFHR3 (Davila et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davila et al., 2010

claim: Three of the five CFHR proteins (CFHR1, 2, and 5) compete with CFH for binding to C3b on heterologous erythrocytes, thereby promoting complement activation.
source: We recently demonstrated that three of the five CFHR proteins (i.e., CFHR1, 2, and 5) compete with CFH for binding to C3b on heterologous erythrocytes, thereby promoting complement activation (Goicoechea de Jorge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goicoechea de Jorge et al., 2013

claim: CFHR3 and CFHR4B both consist of five complement control protein (CCP) domains.
source: We generated full-length CFHR3 and CFHR4B (which both consist of five complement control protein [CCP] domains, Figure 1A)
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: CFHR3 and CFHR4B are CFH antagonists on erythrocyte surfaces.
source: Erythrocyte haemolysis assays demonstrate that CFHR3 and CFHR4B are also CFH antagonists on this surface, with their two C-terminal domains enabling them to compete with CFH for binding sites on cell complement fragments such as C3b (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The two C-terminal domains of CFHR3 and CFHR4B enable them to compete with CFH for binding sites on cell complement fragments such as C3b.
source: Erythrocyte haemolysis assays demonstrate that CFHR3 and CFHR4B are also CFH antagonists on this surface, with their two C-terminal domains enabling them to compete with CFH for binding sites on cell complement fragments such as C3b (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with truncated proteins shown in Figure 1B

claim: Additional cell-surface recognition sites within other domains increase the activity of full-length CFHR3 and CFHR4B as competitive antagonists of CFH.
source: Additional cell-surface recognition sites within other domains (Figure 1A) increase the activity of the full-length CFHR3 and CFHR4B as competitive antagonists of CFH (Figure 1B) at physiologically relevant concentrations of ∼1 μM (Fritsche et al., 2010; Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison of full-length and truncated proteins in haemolysis assays shown in Figure 1B

claim: Physiologically relevant concentrations of CFHR3 and CFHR4B are approximately 1 μM.
source: Additional cell-surface recognition sites within other domains (Figure 1A) increase the activity of the full-length CFHR3 and CFHR4B as competitive antagonists of CFH (Figure 1B) at physiologically relevant concentrations of ∼1 μM (Fritsche et al., 2010; Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fritsche et al., 2010 and Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012

claim: N. meningitidis fHbp recruits CFH by high-affinity interactions primarily with domain 6 of CFH (CFH6) with some limited contact to CFH7.
source: N. meningitidis fHbp recruits CFH by high-affinity interactions primarily with domain 6 of CFH (CFH6) with some limited contact to CFH7 (Schneider et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2009

claim: The first domains of the CFHRs share between 40% to 90% identity with CFH6.
source: Since the first domains of the CFHRs share between 40% to 90% identity with CFH6 (Figure 1A, Figure 2)
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 2

claim: CFHR3 binds fHbp with a KD of approximately 3 nM.
source: Our findings (Figure 1C) demonstrate that CFHR3 binds fHbp with a KD of ∼3 nM, similar to affinities for CFH (Schneider et al., 2009; Johnson et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by SPR and microscale thermophoresis data shown in Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: No significant binding was detected for CFHR1, CFHR2, CFHR4, or CFHR5 with fHbp.
source: no significant binding was detected for the other CFHRs with fHbp.
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The first two domains of CFHR3 (CFHR312) and the full-length protein bind fHbp with similar affinities.
source: Of note, the first two domains of CFHR3 (CFHR312; domain 1 shares 91% identity with CFH6, Figure 1A) and the full-length protein bind fHbp with similar affinities (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by binding affinity measurements shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: Domain 1 of CFHR3 shares 91% identity with CFH6.
source: Of note, the first two domains of CFHR3 (CFHR312; domain 1 shares 91% identity with CFH6, Figure 1A)
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: A point mutation within fHbp (E255A) reduces binding to CFH by more than three orders of magnitude.
source: Furthermore, a point mutation within fHbp (E255A) that reduces binding to CFH by more than three orders of magnitude (Johnson et al., 2012) similarly reduces CFHR3 binding (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2012 and SPR data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The E255A mutation in fHbp similarly reduces CFHR3 binding.
source: Furthermore, a point mutation within fHbp (E255A) that reduces binding to CFH by more than three orders of magnitude (Johnson et al., 2012) similarly reduces CFHR3 binding (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 1E

claim: CFH and CFHR3 occupy overlapping sites on fHbp.
source: The nature of the CFH and CFHR3 interactions with fHbp are therefore similar, with these complement factors occupying overlapping sites on fHbp, which is consistent with the high degree of conservation of their fHbp binding sites (Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from similar binding affinities, effects of E255A mutation, and sequence conservation shown in Figure 2

claim: Serum CFHR3 binds N. meningitidis M1239 in a fHbp-dependent manner.
source: By flow cytometry we demonstrated that serum CFHR3 bound N. meningitidis M1239 (which expresses V3.28 fHbp) in a fHbp-dependent manner. No binding was detected following incubation of bacteria in sera from an individual homozygous for an allele in which there is combined deletion of the CFHR1 and CFHR3 genes (ΔCFHR3/1) (ΔCFHR3/1, Figure 3A,B,C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A,B,C

claim: Addition of full-length CFHR3 results in 51% bacterial survival in normal human serum.
source: Addition of full-length CFHR3 or CFHR312, which contains the fHbp binding site (Figure 1C) but has no CFH antagonist activity (Figure 1B), resulted in significantly reduced bacterial survival (CFHR3 51%; CFHR312 70%; no protein or CFHR345 83%, Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Addition of CFHR312 results in 70% bacterial survival in normal human serum.
source: Addition of full-length CFHR3 or CFHR312, which contains the fHbp binding site (Figure 1C) but has no CFH antagonist activity (Figure 1B), resulted in significantly reduced bacterial survival (CFHR3 51%; CFHR312 70%; no protein or CFHR345 83%, Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Addition of no protein or CFHR345 results in 83% bacterial survival in normal human serum.
source: Addition of full-length CFHR3 or CFHR312, which contains the fHbp binding site (Figure 1C) but has no CFH antagonist activity (Figure 1B), resulted in significantly reduced bacterial survival (CFHR3 51%; CFHR312 70%; no protein or CFHR345 83%, Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: CFHR3 has no detectable effect on bacterial survival in heat-inactivated NHS.
source: in contrast, CFHR3 had no detectable effect in the presence of heat-inactivated NHS (which lacks complement activity, Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Full-length CFHR3 has a more marked effect on bacterial survival than CFHR312.
source: Full-length CFHR3 has a more marked effect on bacterial survival than CFHR312, consistent with the ability of the full-length CHHR3 to bind to C3b deposited on the bacterial surface (via CFHR345) as well as competing with CFH for fHbp (via CFHR312).
evidence: Supported by comparison of bacterial survival data for full-length CFHR3 vs CFHR312 shown in Figure 3D

claim: CFHR345 does not bind fHbp.
source: As CFHR345 does not bind fHbp (Figure 1C), its CFH antagonist activity is not effectively localized to the meningococcal surface, providing an explanation for why these domains have no effect on bacterial survival (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Addition of CFHR3 has no effect on serum survival of bacteria that do not express any CFH-binding protein.
source: Similarly, addition of CFHR3 has no effect on serum survival of bacteria that do not express any CFH-binding protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, N. meningitidis strain lacking fHbp expression; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Escherichia coli strain with no expression of any CFH-binding protein).
evidence: Supported by bacterial survival assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: The majority of mutations in fHbp that impair CFH binding also significantly reduce CFHR3 binding.
source: The results demonstrate that the majority of mutations that impair CFH binding (Johnson et al., 2012) also significantly reduce CFHR3 binding, so do not alter specificity for CFH
evidence: Supported by SPR data for mutant fHbps shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1

claim: Point mutations at only a few sites in fHbp led to modest alterations in specificity for CFH vs CFHR3 at levels that are unlikely to be physiologically relevant.
source: point mutations at only a few sites led to modest alterations in specificity at levels that are unlikely to be physiologically relevant given the relative affinities for CFHR3/CFH and their abundance in serum (CFHR3 1–1.6 μM [Fritsche et al., 2010; Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012]; CFH 1–4 μM [Hakobyan et al., 2008]).
evidence: Supported by SPR data for mutant fHbps and knowledge of physiological concentrations

claim: CFHR3 concentration in serum is 1–1.6 μM.
source: point mutations at only a few sites led to modest alterations in specificity at levels that are unlikely to be physiologically relevant given the relative affinities for CFHR3/CFH and their abundance in serum (CFHR3 1–1.6 μM [Fritsche et al., 2010; Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012]; CFH 1–4 μM [Hakobyan et al., 2008]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fritsche et al., 2010 and Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012

claim: CFH concentration in serum is 1–4 μM.
source: point mutations at only a few sites led to modest alterations in specificity at levels that are unlikely to be physiologically relevant given the relative affinities for CFHR3/CFH and their abundance in serum (CFHR3 1–1.6 μM [Fritsche et al., 2010; Hebecker and Jozsi, 2012]; CFH 1–4 μM [Hakobyan et al., 2008]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hakobyan et al., 2008

claim: V1 fHbp (V1.1) reveals a degree of specificity for CFH over CFHR3 in the order of approximately 20-fold.
source: Interestingly the V1 fHbp used as the background for the mutations (V1.1) did reveal a degree of specificity for CFH over CFHR3 (in the order of ∼20-fold) in contrast to V2 and V3 fHbps, suggesting that certain fHbps can discriminate between CFH and CFHR3.
evidence: Supported by SPR data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1

claim: V2 and V3 fHbps displayed no selective affinity for CFH over CFHR3 with average selectivity being 1.8 ± 1.4 and 2.4 ± 1.0, respectively.
source: This demonstrated that V2 and V3 fHbps displayed no selective affinity for CFH over CFHR3 (average selectivity being 1.8 ± 1.4 and 2.4 ± 1.0, respectively).
evidence: Supported by SPR data for 25 naturally occurring fHbps shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1

claim: V1 fHbps had lower affinities for CFHR3 compared to CFH with average selectivity 8.9 ± 4.6-fold.
source: In contrast, V1 fHbps had lower affinities for CFHR3 compared to CFH (average selectivity 8.9 ± 4.6-fold), with 12 of the 14 V1 fHbp variants binding CFH 5- to 20-fold more tightly than CFHR3.
evidence: Supported by SPR data for 25 naturally occurring fHbps shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1

claim: 12 of the 14 V1 fHbp variants bind CFH 5- to 20-fold more tightly than CFHR3.
source: In contrast, V1 fHbps had lower affinities for CFHR3 compared to CFH (average selectivity 8.9 ± 4.6-fold), with 12 of the 14 V1 fHbp variants binding CFH 5- to 20-fold more tightly than CFHR3.
evidence: Supported by SPR data for 25 naturally occurring fHbps shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1

claim: Bacteria expressing V3.28 fHbp were the most sensitive to alternative pathway killing.
source: Bacteria expressing V3.28 fHbp, which has identical affinities for CFH and CFHR3, were the most sensitive to AP killing, while the strain expressing the V1.1 fHbp sequence (which has ∼20-fold tighter binding to CFH than CFHR3) was the least sensitive; bacteria with fHbps with intermediate CFH specificity displayed intermediate levels of protection.
evidence: Supported by alternative pathway killing assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The strain expressing V1.1 fHbp was the least sensitive to alternative pathway killing.
source: Bacteria expressing V3.28 fHbp, which has identical affinities for CFH and CFHR3, were the most sensitive to AP killing, while the strain expressing the V1.1 fHbp sequence (which has ∼20-fold tighter binding to CFH than CFHR3) was the least sensitive; bacteria with fHbps with intermediate CFH specificity displayed intermediate levels of protection.
evidence: Supported by alternative pathway killing assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Bacteria with fHbps with intermediate CFH specificity displayed intermediate levels of protection from alternative pathway killing.
source: Bacteria expressing V3.28 fHbp, which has identical affinities for CFH and CFHR3, were the most sensitive to AP killing, while the strain expressing the V1.1 fHbp sequence (which has ∼20-fold tighter binding to CFH than CFHR3) was the least sensitive; bacteria with fHbps with intermediate CFH specificity displayed intermediate levels of protection.
evidence: Supported by alternative pathway killing assay data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The ability of fHbp to favour CFH binding promotes bacterial survival.
source: This suggests that, even though the most specific fHbps bind CFHR3 with a KD significantly below the physiological concentration (Figure 4—source data 1), the ability of fHbp to favour CFH binding promotes bacterial survival and offers a potential explanation for the prevalence of strains expressing V1 fHbp causing invasive disease (Lucidarme et al., 2009).
evidence: Inferred from correlation between CFH specificity and bacterial survival shown in Figure 4C

claim: N. meningitidis incubated in ΔCFHR3/1 sera acquire high levels of CFH on the bacterial surface.
source: N. meningitidis incubated in the ΔCFHR3/1 sera acquire high levels of CFH on the bacterial surface (Figure 6A,B,C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B,C

claim: Addition of recombinant CFHR3 reduces the amount of CFH bound to the bacterial surface in a dose-dependent manner.
source: However, addition of recombinant CFHR3 reduces the amount of bound CFH in a dose-dependent manner, demonstrating antagonism between CFH and CFHR3 for binding to the bacterial surface.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B,C

claim: When recombinant CFHR3 is added at approximately equimolar levels to those in NHS, the level of CFH bound on the bacterial surface is only half that seen in CFHR3-deficient sera.
source: When the amount of recombinant CFHR3 is added at approximately equimolar levels to those in NHS, the level of CFH bound on the bacterial surface is only half that seen in the CFHR3-deficient sera (1–1.6 μM [Fritsche et al., 2010]).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A,B,C

claim: Susceptibility to meningococcal disease is governed by the competition between CFH and CFHR3 for overlapping binding sites on fHbp.
source: In summary, our work demonstrates that susceptibility to an important infectious disease is governed by the competition between two complement factors with opposing effects (CFH and CFHR3) for overlapping binding sites on a single pathogen molecule.
evidence: Supported by the collective experimental data showing competition between CFH and CFHR3 for fHbp binding and effects on bacterial survival

claim: The risk of developing meningococcal disease is governed by the relative abundance of CFH and CFHR3 in individuals and the affinity of these molecules for the specific fHbp on the bacterial surface.
source: Our data predict that the risk of developing meningococcal disease will be governed by the relative abundance of CFH and CFHR3 in individuals and the affinity of these molecules for the specific fHbp on the bacterial surface (Figure 6D).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing effects of CFH/CFHR3 ratio and fHbp variant on bacterial survival

claim: The ΔCFHR3/1 allele has a high prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: It is notable that the ΔCFHR3/1 allele has a high prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa (Holmes et al., 2013) where there are high rates of epidemic disease.
evidence: Supported by citation to Holmes et al., 2013

claim: Sub-Saharan Africa has high rates of epidemic meningococcal disease.
source: It is notable that the ΔCFHR3/1 allele has a high prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa (Holmes et al., 2013) where there are high rates of epidemic disease.
evidence: Supported by general knowledge and citation context

claim: The ΔCFHR3/1 allele would enhance the interaction between CFH and fHbp and favour pathogen survival.
source: Our mechanism is consistent with this association, since this allele would enhance the interaction between CFH and fHbp and favour pathogen survival.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that absence of CFHR3 increases CFH binding to bacteria

claim: The ΔCFHR3/1 deletion is associated with increased plasma CFH levels.
source: This is particularly true as the ΔCFHR3/1 deletion is associated with increased plasma CFH levels, most likely due to the loss of a regulatory locus (Ansari et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ansari et al., 2013 and Zhu et al., 2014

claim: Host polymorphisms in CFHR3 might have less impact on strains of bacteria that express fHbp that more selectively bind CFH.
source: However, host polymorphisms in CFHR3 might have less impact on strains of bacteria that express fHbp that more selectively bind CFH.
evidence: Inferred from data showing V1 fHbps have greater specificity for CFH and provide better protection

claim: Susceptibility to meningococcal disease is influenced by polymorphisms and copy number variation affecting CFH and CFHR3 and by the relative affinity of fHbp on an infecting strain for CFH and CFHR3.
source: Therefore, susceptibility to meningococcal disease will be influenced by polymorphisms and copy number variation affecting two host complement factors and by the relative affinity of fHbp on an infecting strain for CFH and CFHR3.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental data showing both host and pathogen factors affect disease susceptibility

claim: Genetic association studies in infectious diseases are likely to be technically challenging since these will be influenced not only by sequence and structural variation within the host but also by genetic variation in pathogen.
source: This illustrates why genetic association studies in infectious diseases are likely to be technically challenging since these will be influenced not only by sequence and structural variation within the host but also by genetic variation in pathogen.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that both host (CFH/CFHR3) and pathogen (fHbp variant) factors affect disease susceptibility

claim: Natural fHbp sequences are relatively constant in their KD for CFH at approximately 3 nM.
source: Natural fHbp sequences are relatively constant in their KD for CFH (KD ∼3 nM [Johnson et al., 2012] and this work)
evidence: Supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2012 and SPR data in this work

claim: CFHR312 has no CFH antagonist activity.
source: Addition of full-length CFHR3 or CFHR312, which contains the fHbp binding site (Figure 1C) but has no CFH antagonist activity (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The two N-terminal CCP domains from CFHR3 had no effect on erythrocyte haemolysis.
source: The two N-terminal CCP domains from CFHR3 had no effect (not shown).
evidence: Stated as experimental observation

claim: CFHR3 alone does not cause significant haemolysis of guinea pig erythrocytes in CFH depleted serum.
source: Haemolysis of guinea pig erythrocytes by 5% CFH depleted serum (CompTech, TX, USA) was measured upon addition of a range of CFHR3 concentrations (4 nM–2 μM) in Mg-EGTA to ensure activation by the alternative pathway (AP) alone. Haemolysis is presented as a percentage of maximal lysis by H2O. No significant differences in haemolysis were observed under any of the conditions.
evidence: Supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Addition of 2 mM CFHR3 to CFH-supplemented serum led to a significant increase in haemolysis.
source: Supplementing the CFH deficient serum (CompTech, TX, USA) with 100 nM CFH reduced lysis to ∼20%. In this CFH-supplemented experiment addition of 2 mM CFHR3 led to a significant (p = 0.003, two-tailed, unpaired t test) increase in haemolysis as seen with the naturally CFH sufficient serum in Figure 1.
evidence: Supported by haemolysis assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Full-length CFHR3 interacts strongly with the carboxymethyldextran matrix used to immobilise proteins in SPR.
source: Full-length CFHR3 interacts strongly with the carboxymethyldextran matrix used to immobilise proteins in SPR, therefore, microscale thermophoeresis (Seidel et al., 2013), a solution technique, was used to measure the affinity for V3.28 fHbp.
evidence: Stated as experimental observation and justification for method choice

claim: There are only two conservative sequence differences between CFH67 and CFHR312 found in the fHbp binding site.
source: Looking down onto the fHbp binding site on CFH the two, conservative, sequence differences between the CFH67 and CFHR312 found in the binding site are indicated in red on the grey surface.
evidence: Shown in sequence alignment in Figure 2A and structural representation in Figure 2D

claim: V1 fHbps are prevalent in strains causing invasive meningococcal disease.
source: the ability of fHbp to favour CFH binding promotes bacterial survival and offers a potential explanation for the prevalence of strains expressing V1 fHbp causing invasive disease (Lucidarme et al., 2009).
evidence: Implied by the statement about prevalence and supported by citation to Lucidarme et al., 2009
